lessons.title: Common Weeds and Their Impact on Yield
lessons.body:
Weeds are the silent thieves of your sweet potato harvest. In Africa, the most damaging weeds include couch grass (Agropyron repens), pigweed (Amaranthus spp.), blackjack (Bidens pilosa), and nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus). These weeds compete with your crop for water, nutrients, and sunlight. Research from Kenya and Nigeria shows that unchecked weeds can reduce sweet potato yields by 30 to 60 percent. For example, a plot that could produce 10 tonnes per hectare may yield only 4 tonnes if weeds are left to grow.

The first 6 to 8 weeks after planting are critical. Sweet potato vines spread slowly at first, leaving plenty of open soil for weeds to take over. Couch grass is especially bad because its underground stems (rhizomes) regrow even after you pull the top. Nutgrass is called the world's worst weed because it pierces through tubers, making them unsellable. Pigweed grows fast and tall, shading your vines.

Weeds also harbour pests and diseases. Aphids and whiteflies often live on weeds before moving to your sweet potatoes. Some weeds, like blackjack, can host viruses that later infect your crop. So weed control is not just about removing competition; it is also about breaking the pest cycle.

To measure impact, do a simple test: mark two 1m x 1m squares in your field. Keep one weed-free for the first 8 weeks, and leave the other unweeded. At harvest, dig up both squares and weigh the tubers. You will see the difference yourself. On average, each kilogram of weed dry matter per square meter can reduce tuber yield by 0.5 to 1 kilogram. So if you have 2 kg of weeds per square meter, you could lose 1 to 2 tonnes per hectare. That is money lost. Therefore, plan to weed early and often.

lessons.title: Integrated Weed Management: Cultural, Mechanical, Chemical
lessons.body:
Integrated Weed Management (IWM) means using a combination of methods to control weeds, rather than relying on one. This is cheaper, safer, and more effective. The three main pillars are cultural, mechanical, and chemical control.

Cultural control starts before you plant. Choose a field with low weed pressure. If you have a weedy field, plant a cover crop like cowpea or mucuna for one season to smother weeds. Rotate sweet potatoes with maize or beans; different crops have different growth habits that disrupt weed cycles. Also, plant sweet potato vines denselyâspacing of 30 cm between plants and 1 m between ridgesâso the vines cover the ground faster and shade out weeds.

Mechanical control is hand weeding, hoeing, or using a hand cultivator. In Africa, most smallholders weed by hand. Do your first weeding 2 to 3 weeks after planting, and a second 5 to 6 weeks after planting. After that, the vines should cover the ground. Be careful not to damage the shallow roots of sweet potatoes. A sharp hoe used shallowly (2-3 cm deep) is best. You can also use a mower between ridges if you have one. Never weed when the soil is wetâit spreads weed seeds and compacts soil.

Chemical control uses herbicides, but only as a last resort. For sweet potatoes, few herbicides are registered in many African countries. Glyphosate can be used before planting to kill existing weeds, but it must be applied 2 weeks before planting and not after. Metribuzin can be applied after planting but before vines spread, at 0.5 kg per hectare. Always read the label and wear protective clothing. Never use herbicides near water sources.

Combine all three: start with cultural methods, add mechanical weeding, and use chemicals only on tough spots. This reduces costs and keeps your soil healthy.

lessons.title: Major Insect Pests: Sweet Potato Weevil, Whiteflies, and Aphids
lessons.body:
Three insect pests cause the most damage to sweet potatoes in Africa: sweet potato weevil, whiteflies, and aphids. Learn to identify them and act early.

The sweet potato weevil (Cylas spp.) is the worst. It is a small, ant-like beetle, 5-7 mm long, with a dark body and orange legs. The female lays eggs in the soil near the roots or on the vines. The larvae bore into the tubers, making tunnels and causing a bitter taste. A single weevil can ruin a whole tuber. You will see small holes on the tuber surface and black spots inside. Weevils also attack vines, causing them to wilt. In Africa, weevil damage can reach 50-80% of the harvest if uncontrolled. Control: use clean planting material (vines from uninfested fields), crop rotation with maize or beans, and harvest promptly. You can also use pheromone traps (available in some countries) or apply neem extract.

Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) are tiny, white, moth-like insects that suck sap from leaves. They excrete honeydew, which causes sooty mould, reducing photosynthesis. More importantly, they transmit viruses like sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus. You will see whiteflies swarming when you shake the vines. Control: plant resistant varieties, use yellow sticky traps, and spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil every 7 days.

Aphids (Myzus persicae) are small, green or black, and cluster on young leaves and stems. They also transmit viruses. They multiply fastâone aphid can become hundreds in a week. Control: encourage ladybirds and lacewings (natural predators), spray with a strong jet of water, or use neem oil. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which makes plants more attractive to aphids.

Scout your field weekly. Look under leaves and on stems. Early action saves your crop.

lessons.title: Common Diseases: Fusarium Wilt, Black Rot, and Viral Infections
lessons.body:
Sweet potatoes suffer from several diseases, but three are most common in Africa: Fusarium wilt, black rot, and viral infections.

Fusarium wilt is caused by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. batatas. It lives in the soil and enters through roots. Symptoms: leaves turn yellow, then brown, and wilt. The inside of the stem shows brown streaks. The plant may die within 2 weeks. The fungus can survive in soil for up to 5 years. Control: use resistant varieties (like 'Tanzania' or 'SPK004'), rotate with maize or sorghum for at least 3 years, and remove and burn infected plants. Do not compost diseased plants.

Black rot is caused by the fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata. It affects tubers in storage and in the field. Symptoms: small, dark, sunken spots on tubers that expand into large black lesions. The rot smells sweet and fruity. It spreads through wounds during harvest. Control: handle tubers gently to avoid cuts, cure tubers in a warm, dry place for 5-7 days before storage, and store in a cool, ventilated area. Dip tubers in hot water (50Â°C for 5 minutes) before storage to kill spores. Never store bruised or damaged tubers.

Viral infections are caused by viruses like Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chlorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV). They are spread by aphids and whiteflies, or through infected vines. Symptoms: leaves show yellow mottling, vein clearing, or purple rings. Plants are stunted and produce small tubers. There is no cure. Control: use virus-free planting material (certified vines from tissue culture or clean nurseries), control aphids and whiteflies, and remove infected plants immediately. In Africa, up to 90% of yield loss can occur when both viruses combine (virus synergy).

Always source vines from a trusted clean seed system. If you see symptoms, uproot and burn the plant. Do not save vines from a diseased field.

lessons.title: Biological and Chemical Control Options
lessons.body:
When pests and diseases get out of hand, you can use biological or chemical controls. Biological control uses living organisms to fight pests. Chemical control uses synthetic pesticides. Both have a place, but biological is safer and cheaper for smallholders.

Biological control options: Neem extract is the most widely used. Crush 1 kg of neem seeds, soak in 10 litres of water for 24 hours, strain, and spray. It repels and kills aphids, whiteflies, and weevil larvae. Apply every 7-10 days. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a bacterium that kills caterpillars but not bees. It is sold as a powder and mixed with water. For sweet potato weevil, you can use the fungus Beauveria bassiana, which infects and kills the weevil. Mix 10 g of powder per litre of water and spray on soil around plants. Ladybirds, lacewings, and parasitic wasps are natural predatorsâavoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill them.

Chemical control options: Use only when biological methods fail and pest pressure is high. For sweet potato weevil, apply chlorpyrifos (e.g., Dursban) at 2 litres per hectare in the soil before planting. For aphids and whiteflies, spray imidacloprid (e.g., Confidor) at 0.5 litres per hectare. For Fusarium wilt, there is no effective chemical; use resistant varieties. For black rot, dip tubers in benomyl (0.5 g per litre) before storage. Always wear gloves, mask, and long sleeves. Follow the label exactly. Do not spray within 7 days of harvest. Never mix chemicals unless the label says so.

Remember: chemicals can harm your health and the environment. Use them as a last resort. Rotate chemicals to prevent resistance. Store them locked away from children and animals.

lessons.title: Implementing Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Strategies
lessons.body:
Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is a decision-making process that combines all control methods to keep pests and diseases below damaging levels. It is not about eliminating all pests; it is about managing them economically and safely.

The first step is prevention. Use clean planting material from certified sources. Rotate cropsânever plant sweet potatoes in the same field two seasons in a row. Plant resistant varieties like 'Kabode' or 'Naspot 1' where available. Keep your field free of weeds that harbour pests. Space plants properly to allow air movement, which reduces fungal diseases.

The second step is monitoring. Scout your field every week. Walk in a zigzag pattern and check 10 random plants. Look for weevil holes, whiteflies, aphids, yellow leaves, or wilting. Write down what you see. Use pheromone traps for weevils (1 trap per 100 square meters) and yellow sticky traps for whiteflies (10 traps per hectare). When pest numbers exceed thresholdsâfor example, 5 aphids per leaf or 10% of plants with weevil damageâtake action.

The third step is intervention. Start with biological controls: neem spray, Bt, or Beauveria. If those fail, use mechanical methods: handpick weevils, remove infected plants, or use a strong water spray for aphids. Only if pest pressure is still high, use chemicals. Always choose the least toxic option and spot-treat affected areas rather than spraying the whole field.

Record everything: what you saw, what you did, and the results. This helps you make better decisions next season. Share your records with other farmers. IPM reduces costs, protects your health, and gives you a better harvest. Start smallâtry one IPM practice this season and see the difference.

quiz.q: Which weed is known as the world's worst weed because it pierces sweet potato tubers?
quiz.explanation: Nutgrass (Cyperus rotundus) has sharp rhizomes that penetrate tubers, making them unsellable.

quiz.q: How much can unchecked weeds reduce sweet potato yield?
quiz.explanation: Research shows weeds can cause 30-60% yield loss in sweet potatoes.

quiz.q: What is the critical weeding period for sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato vines spread slowly, so weeds compete most in the first 6-8 weeks.

quiz.q: Which method is NOT part of Integrated Weed Management?
quiz.explanation: IWM combines cultural, mechanical, and chemical methods; ignoring weeds is not a method.

quiz.q: What is a good cultural practice to reduce weeds before planting sweet potatoes?
options: A) Plant cover crops like mucuna
quiz.explanation: Cover crops smother weeds and add organic matter.

quiz.q: When is the best time to do the first hand weeding?
quiz.explanation: First weeding should be done 2-3 weeks after planting to remove early weeds.

quiz.q: Which herbicide can be used before planting sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate is a non-selective herbicide applied before planting to kill existing weeds.

quiz.q: What is the most damaging insect pest of sweet potatoes in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato weevil (Cylas spp.) causes up to 80% yield loss.

quiz.q: How can you identify sweet potato weevil damage in tubers?
options: B) Small holes and black spots inside
quiz.explanation: Weevil larvae bore into tubers, creating holes and black spots.

quiz.q: What do whiteflies transmit to sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Whiteflies transmit viruses like sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus.

quiz.q: Which natural predator helps control aphids?
quiz.explanation: Ladybirds and lacewings are natural predators of aphids.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to control aphids without chemicals?
options: A) Spray with strong water jet
quiz.explanation: A strong water spray dislodges aphids from leaves.

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. batatas?
quiz.explanation: Fusarium wilt is caused by this soil-borne fungus.

quiz.q: What are symptoms of Fusarium wilt in sweet potatoes?
options: A) Yellow leaves and brown streaks in stem
quiz.explanation: Fusarium wilt causes yellowing, wilting, and brown vascular streaks.

quiz.q: How long can Fusarium wilt fungus survive in soil?
quiz.explanation: The fungus can survive in soil for up to 5 years.

quiz.q: What causes black rot in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Black rot is caused by the fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata.

quiz.q: How can you prevent black rot during storage?
quiz.explanation: Curing tubers in warm, dry conditions helps heal wounds and prevent rot.

quiz.q: What is a hot water treatment for black rot?
options: B) Dip in 50Â°C water for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Hot water at 50Â°C for 5 minutes kills fungal spores on tuber surfaces.

quiz.q: Which viruses cause viral infections in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Sweet Potato Feathery Mottle Virus (SPFMV) and Sweet Potato Chlorotic Stunt Virus (SPCSV) are common.

quiz.q: How are viral infections spread in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Aphids and whiteflies transmit sweet potato viruses.

quiz.q: What is the best control for viral infections?
quiz.explanation: There is no cure; using clean vines is the main control.

quiz.q: Which biological control agent kills sweet potato weevil larvae?
quiz.explanation: Beauveria bassiana is a fungus that infects and kills weevils.

quiz.q: How do you prepare neem extract for spraying?
options: A) Soak neem leaves in water for 1 hour
B) Crush 1 kg neem seeds in 10 L water for 24 hours
D) Mix neem oil with soap
quiz.explanation: Crushing neem seeds and soaking in water releases the active compounds.

quiz.q: Which chemical is recommended for sweet potato weevil control?
quiz.explanation: Chlorpyrifos is applied to soil to control weevil larvae.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval for most chemicals used on sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Most labels require at least 7 days between spraying and harvest.

quiz.q: What is the first step in Integrated Pest Management?
quiz.explanation: IPM starts with prevention through clean planting material and crop rotation.

quiz.q: How often should you scout your sweet potato field for pests?
quiz.explanation: Weekly scouting helps detect pests early.

quiz.q: What is a pheromone trap used for?
quiz.explanation: Pheromone traps attract and trap male weevils.

quiz.q: What is the threshold for aphid infestation before taking action?
quiz.explanation: Action threshold is about 5 aphids per leaf to prevent virus spread.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in IPM?
options: B) To make better decisions next season
quiz.explanation: Records help you learn what works and improve your management.
